prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 regime

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks, credited to Katori and Ye. After round 1 I have tested it against the chair's questions rather than on the strength of the opening count. The decisive idea is that a trapping wavelength can be chosen so that the light shift is identical for both clock states, which removes Doppler and recoil shifts while thousands of atoms are interrogated in parallel. That is a statement about how to make an atom a clean quantum system, and it is distinct from the 2005 prize (combs as a frequency ruler) and the 2012 prize (control of single trapped quantum systems). A citation can say this precisely by naming magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms. The consequences are physics as well as engineering: independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST agree at the 1e-18 level, gravitational redshift has been resolved across millimetre height differences inside a single atomic sample, and clock comparisons already give bounds on drifts of constants and on some ultralight dark-matter couplings. Those bounds are real but not yet decisive, and I say so openly below. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori for the concept and the first strontium demonstrations, Ye for carrying accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics to the frontier.
statement.case_against: The most serious objection, which I take as a real one, is that this is chiefly a measurement achievement. No deviation from general relativity or the Standard Model has been found with lattice clocks, so the fundamental-physics payoff consists of bounds and enabling capability, not a discovery that nature behaves differently from expectation. The committee has also twice honoured neighbouring ground (2005, 2012), and Ye's comb-linked comparisons could be read as an extension of Hall and Haensch. Credit is not exclusive: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Derevianko, the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups and the Al+ ion-clock tradition all contributed, and a two-name credit cannot absorb them. I should record why they fall outside it: the magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstration of the neutral-atom lattice clock are Katori's, and the sustained advance to the 1e-18 regime with the accompanying many-body clock work is Ye's, while the others refined, extended or rebuilt these. I cannot exclude that expert reports would argue for a different attribution. Finally, as a theorist in a neighbouring field I may overrate clean, controllable quantum systems.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that the discovery of a new class of quantum matter (topological insulators) should weigh more heavily than a further gain in precision, and that my own arguments of maturity and reproducibility apply at least as strongly to B007.
responses.response: I accept the first half. Maturity and reproducibility do apply to topological insulators, and I do not claim they separate the two cases. Where I still differ is attribution and framing. You name the omission of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu as the real weak point of B007, and that is not a small matter: the HgTe proposal that Molenkamp tested came from them, and the three-dimensional case rests on others again. For the clocks, I would argue the claim is not merely continuity with 2005. The magic-wavelength lattice is a new way of preparing a many-atom quantum system, and it opened a new regime of measurement. Your point that new matter outweighs better precision is a legitimate value judgment, but I would not make it decisive when the credit cannot be drawn within three names. I keep B007 as an alternative and I defer to you on how large the overlap with the 2016 topology prize is.

responses.point: Eriksson asks whether lattice clocks give a new state or behaviour of matter or are mainly a measurement achievement, and says B054 offers more new physics per unit time, but would not oppose B042 if the AMO members find the attribution clean.
responses.response: This is the fairest framing of the dispute, and in the narrow sense I concede it: the clock is a measurement achievement, not a new phase. The AMO attribution is, to my reading, clean for two names, which was your condition, so I take your statement as non-opposition. On B054 my reservation remains maturity, not importance. The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction is impressive and the 2018 experiments were decisive, but the pairing mechanism is open and twist-angle disorder still limits what is intrinsic. If the committee returns to it in a few years, I would support the MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero shape you propose over a three-name credit with Bistritzer. I do not regard speed of confirmation as unimportant, but fast reproduction of the phenomenon is not the same as a settled interpretation.

responses.point: Danielsson conditions his support for B042 on whether lattice-clock comparisons have produced competitive bounds on constants, dark matter or gravity, and notes that Al+ ion clocks may be a co-equal claim.
responses.response: Here is my best answer to the chair's question. Optical clock comparisons, mostly Sr, Yb and ion systems, have set stringent limits on temporal drift of the fine-structure constant and of the electron-to-proton mass ratio, and have constrained couplings of ultralight scalar dark matter in specific mass windows. The millimetre-scale redshift measurement is a direct laboratory test of a general-relativity prediction. These are competitive within their niches but they are null results, and I do not want to oversell them as discoveries. On Al+, I think the ion-clock tradition is a different physical route: single-ion clocks avoid the many-atom problem rather than solving it, and the 2012 prize already covered the control of single ions. I would not claim the Al+ groups have no standing, but I do not see them as a rival for the magic-wavelength idea. I will accept that your condition is met in the sense of existing bounds and not met in the sense of a discovery.

responses.point: Pearce says the citation must rest on the lattice trapping concept and the 1e-18 regime it opened, not on clocks or combs in general, and that the committee should record why Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow fall outside a two-name credit.
responses.response: I agree and have changed my citation accordingly: it now names magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms explicitly, so that it does not read as re-rewarding combs or single-ion control. On recording the exclusions, I have set out above what I would put in the minutes: Katori made the proposal and the first demonstration, Ye took the system to the accuracy and stability frontier, and the other groups, including Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow, are important contributors who refined the approach and reached the same regime later. If expert reports identify a primary-literature contribution that precedes or is co-equal with Katori's proposal, I would reopen the third name, but I have not seen that evidence, and I would not add a name without it.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues are persuaded that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct idea and not a successor step to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.

Whether expert reports on the primary literature would identify a third contributor (an early magic-wavelength theory or the Lemonde or ytterbium work) with a claim as strong as the two named; I rely partly on memory here.
How far the weight on a null-result, bounds-only fundamental-physics payoff should count in a prize for a discovery.
Whether the formal redefinition of the second, or nuclear (thorium-229) or ion-clock developments, would make a later configuration more natural.
statement.conflict_note: My disclosure from round 1 is unchanged. I direct WACQT and work at Chalmers MC2 in superconducting quantum circuits, and I have a personal collaboration in phonon and artificial-atom work that touches B023 (optomechanics, Cleland); I would recuse myself from any configuration that includes B023, which no member now proposes. I have no connection to Katori or Ye. Kroll sits on the WACQT executive management team and Olsson is a Chalmers colleague; I regard these as institutional overlaps, not conflicts, and none affects my judgment on B042. I note my own bias toward clean controllable quantum systems and have tried to discount it.
